items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I went to see one of the best Negro lawyers in town, a fellow by the name of Bailey and he told me that I could get a divorce for 35 dollars

ctx.x: Edgar James and William Smith, drummer and pianist respectively, were the only two musicians other than Page still around Cincinnati that I had played with at the beginning of my career. Wes Helvey who had been the second band leader I had worked with in Cincinnati had quite the game, moved to Detroit, and was in the insurance business. I was considered a star trumpet man with Page because I had lived in New York and made a name among the musicians. Nobody knew the real reason for my coming back home except…

I went to see one of the best Negro lawyers in town, a fellow by the name of Bailey and he told me that I could get a divorce for 35 dollars but I would have to stay in Cincinnati for three months before I could apply for it. It was the month of June 1935, that I had come home. I gigged with Clarence Page and we played the Lexington, Kentucky fair in July. My father decided to move into a larger apartment because he liked Beezie very much and thought that she and I would stay in Cincinnati if we had more rooms.

We moved to 9th street near the Shermann school which was the first school I had gone to when my mother was living with Aunt Mary, which was between Mound and John Streets. There was three rooms, kitchen and bath on the second floor of a three-story house. Tommy Smith the drummer
